flows.title: Direct chat
flows.narration: A signed-in user sends one message; the request crosses Cloudflare and Traefik to OpenWebUI, which streams a reply directly from the resident llama-server.

steps.narration: A user opens medchat in their browser and types a question. When they press enter, the browser sends an HTTPS POST to medchat.peyman.io. The request carries a session cookie that proves the user is signed in — it was set earlier when they logged in through the OpenID Connect single-sign-on flow.

The request reaches Cloudflare first. Because the homelab keeps every public port closed, Cloudflare cannot connect to it directly. Instead, a Cloudflare Tunnel that the homelab opened earlier pipes the request safely inward, delivering it onto the internal platform-net Docker network.

Inside the homelab, Traefik is the gatekeeper that decides which container serves which hostname. It reads the request's Host: medchat.peyman.io header and forwards the request to the open-webui container listening on port 8080.

OpenWebUI is the chat user interface. No tools are involved on this turn, so it simply forwards the question to the local language model. It calls llama-server using the OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions API, asking the resident model (alias 'medchat') for a reply.
steps.note: No tool server attached on this turn. (src=ops/setup-openwebui.sh:88)

steps.narration: llama-server runs MedGemma-4B (a 4-billion-parameter open medical model) on the homelab's GPU. As soon as the model starts producing tokens, llama-server streams them back to OpenWebUI one at a time over Server-Sent Events (SSE), so the user does not have to wait for the entire reply.
steps.payload: Server-sent events with assistant content deltas.

steps.narration: OpenWebUI relays the streamed tokens out to the browser, where the answer appears word by word. Before display, a small filter called strip_tool_chips scrubs any leftover tool-call markup from the text, so the reader only sees clean prose.
steps.payload: Rendered markdown back through Traefik and Cloudflare.

flows.name: Direct chat
flows.tagline: The simplest path. A question goes in, an answer comes back, no tools in the middle.

flows.title: Tools chat
flows.narration: OpenWebUI discovers the tool server's OpenAPI schema, the local model emits a tool call, OpenWebUI dispatches it to medchat-mcp, and the model writes the cited answer in a follow-up turn.

steps.narration: A user asks a medical question with the MedChat Tools server enabled. The request reaches OpenWebUI by the same path as a direct chat — Cloudflare, then Traefik, then the container — but this time tools are in play.
steps.payload: Chat turn through Cloudflare and Traefik.

steps.narration: Before forwarding the question to the model, OpenWebUI fetches the catalogue of available tools from medchat-mcp. FastAPI publishes that catalogue automatically as an OpenAPI schema at /openapi.json. Every endpoint listed there becomes a tool the model can choose.
OpenWebUI now calls llama-server, but along with the user's question it attaches the tool definitions. The model is effectively told: 'these are the functions you can call if you need help.'

The model reads the question, decides it needs evidence from the literature, and returns a tool_call instead of a plain answer. The tool_call names the function (pubmed_search) and supplies the JSON arguments to call it with (for example {query, top_k:5}).
OpenWebUI is responsible for actually running the tool. It POSTs the model's arguments to medchat-mcp at /tools/pubmed_search. The model itself never touches the network — OpenWebUI is its hands.
steps.payload: POST /tools/pubmed_search with the model's JSON arguments.

steps.narration: medchat-mcp executes the search by calling NCBI's E-utilities, the public HTTP API behind PubMed. Soft and hard timeouts come from MEDCHAT_TOOL_TIMEOUT_*_MS, so a slow upstream cannot hang the whole turn.

NCBI returns raw JSON. medchat-mcp normalizes it into a ToolResult of the form {results: [...], note?: '...'}. By contract, tools never return a 5xx error — if NCBI is slow or broken, the result is simply an empty list with a descriptive note.
steps.payload: Raw JSON normalized into ToolResult{results, note}.

steps.narration: The ToolResult travels back to OpenWebUI as an ordinary HTTP response. OpenWebUI now has structured evidence to hand back to the model.
OpenWebUI calls llama-server again, this time appending the tool result as an extra message. The model can now read what was found and write the actual answer.
steps.payload: Follow-up POST with the tool message appended.

steps.narration: The model writes the final reply, weaving in citation markers like [PubMed:12345] to point at the papers it relied on.
OpenWebUI sends the reply out to the browser. A filter called citation_links rewrites every marker into a numbered hyperlink and appends a Sources panel listing every cited paper.

flows.name: Tools chat
flows.tagline: The local model decides it needs help. It calls a medical tool, then writes its answer.

flows.title: Cloud consult (REST)
flows.narration: A caller POSTs to medchat-mcp; the orchestrator drives Claude Sonnet through a bounded tool loop, citecheck strips uncited claims, and the final envelope returns with sources.

steps.narration: A caller — an external script, a curl command, or OpenWebUI in cloud-only mode — POSTs to medchat-mcp at /v1/chat/completions with the standard OpenAI-shaped body {messages, format}. If external auth is enabled, the request must carry a bearer token from MEDCHAT_API_KEYS.

medchat-mcp asks Claude Sonnet (the cloud LLM) to think about the question. It does this through nexus-router, an in-house OpenAI-compatible proxy that holds the cloud credentials. The call carries the full tool catalogue (TOOL_DEFS) and tool_choice='auto', leaving Sonnet free to decide which tools to use. The entire orchestration loop is capped at three rounds, so a confused model cannot run forever.
Sonnet replies. Either it has chosen its final answer (the loop ends), or it asks medchat-mcp to run one or more tools first.
steps.payload: Either content or tool_calls to dispatch.

steps.narration: medchat-mcp executes each requested tool. Depending on what Sonnet asked for, this fans out to PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, openFDA, RxNav, or Europe PMC — the medical APIs medchat-mcp wraps.
The tool results are sent back to Sonnet as a follow-up message. Armed with this evidence, Sonnet drafts the user-facing answer and signals that the loop can end.
steps.payload: Next round with tool messages appended.

steps.narration: Before the answer reaches the user, an internal gate called citecheck inspects it. citecheck builds an EvidencePack from this turn's tool results, then walks the draft sentence by sentence. Any factual sentence without a matching citation marker is stripped out. A pack hash is recorded for the audit log, and the rolling stub-rate is updated.
steps.payload: EvidencePack built from tool results; uncited sentences removed; pack_hash computed.

steps.narration: The cleaned answer leaves medchat-mcp wrapped in metadata: the answer text, a list of structured sources, the citation markers themselves, and a meta object describing whether the safety stub was used, how many orchestration rounds ran, and the total latency in milliseconds.
steps.payload: ChatCompletionOut{answer, sources, citations, meta{stub_used, rounds, latency_ms}}.

flows.name: Cloud consult (REST)
flows.tagline: The heaviest path. medchat-mcp orchestrates Claude Sonnet through a tool loop, then checks every citation.

flows.title: MCP consult
flows.narration: An external MCP client opens an SSE channel to /mcp and invokes medchat_consult; the orchestrator runs the same tool loop and streams the response back through the channel.

steps.narration: An external MCP client — for example, an automation script or another agent that speaks Model Context Protocol — opens a Server-Sent Events channel to medchat-mcp at /mcp. Through that channel it invokes the tool medchat_consult({question, format}). Same orchestrator, different doorway.
Internally, medchat-mcp runs the exact same Claude Sonnet tool-calling loop used by the REST endpoint. Reusing the orchestrator means MCP callers and REST callers can never drift apart.
Sonnet's tool calls fan out to the medical APIs (PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, openFDA, RxNav, Europe PMC), just as they do in the REST flow.

The final answer is streamed back over the same SSE channel. Callers that asked for format='text' receive plain prose; callers that asked for format='json' receive the full envelope of answer, sources, citations, and metadata.
steps.payload: Plain text (format='text') or full JSON envelope (format='json').

flows.name: MCP consult
flows.tagline: An external MCP client calls medchat_consult over SSE. Same loop, different doorway.

flows.title: RAG search
flows.narration: medchat-mcp embeds the query with Ollama, runs a cosine-distance lookup in pgvector, and returns the top-k chunks tagged with [RAG:<chunk_id>] markers.

steps.narration: Some caller (OpenWebUI, the orchestrator, or an MCP client) POSTs to /tools/rag_search with a natural-language query, a top-k count, and an optional corpus filter such as 'dailymed' or 'cdc'.

medchat-mcp cannot search by meaning on its own — it needs a vector. It asks Ollama (the homelab embedder daemon) to produce one: POST /api/embed with model qwen3-embedding:8b returns a 4096-dimensional float vector. If Ollama is unreachable, medchat-mcp returns an empty ToolResult with note='embed_unavailable' rather than failing the whole turn.

With the vector in hand, medchat-mcp runs a cosine-similarity search against the seeded corpus in PostgreSQL. The pgvector extension's <=> operator computes the distance between the query vector and each stored chunk's halfvec embedding. ORDER BY ... LIMIT :k returns the k closest matches.
steps.payload: ORDER BY embedding <=> halfvec(:qv) LIMIT :k from medchat_rag.chunk.

steps.narration: PostgreSQL hands back the top-k chunks, each with its cosine similarity score, source title, public URL, and corpus name.
medchat-mcp wraps those rows into a ToolResult. Each chunk gets a citation marker like [RAG:<chunk_id>] so that citecheck can later validate any sentence that refers to it.

flows.name: RAG search
flows.tagline: Embed the question, then find the nearest chunks in pgvector by cosine similarity. This flow is reused inside other flows whenever the model picks the rag_search tool.

flows.title: Attached file
flows.narration: medchat-mcp asks files-service for the snippets relevant to a previously uploaded document and forwards them back to OpenWebUI as a ToolResult.

steps.narration: When a user has uploaded a file, the model can call attached_file_search. OpenWebUI POSTs the file id, the query, and how many chunks to return.

medchat-mcp does not store the file or its embeddings — files-service does. medchat-mcp simply proxies the request: POST {FILES_SERVICE_URL}/v1/files/{file_id}/retrieve, authenticated with the per-service bearer token FILES_SERVICE_TOKEN_MEDCHAT.

files-service runs its own chunking and sqlite-vec retrieval on the uploaded document, then returns the top-k snippets. If the file id does not exist, the 404 becomes a soft note='not found'; if the token is wrong, the 401 or 403 becomes a degraded note. medchat-mcp never bubbles a 5xx error to the caller.
The snippets travel back to OpenWebUI as a ToolResult, ready for the model to read in its next round.

flows.name: Attached file
flows.tagline: A user-uploaded document. medchat-mcp asks files-service for the relevant chunks.

flows.title: citecheck gate
flows.narration: Every cloud answer flows through citecheck: quiesce check, evidence-pack rebuild, marker resolution, observation update.

steps.narration: The cloud orchestrator has just produced a draft answer, and it is holding every tool result returned during this turn. Before the draft can reach the user, the orchestrator hands the bundle — {draft_text, tool_results, ok_tools, failed_tools} — to the citecheck egress gate.

First, citecheck asks the in-memory auto-quiesce singleton whether the system is in degraded mode. If more than 15% of answers in the last 24 hours have been served as the safety stub, citecheck does not even look at the draft — it immediately returns the canned 'evidence incomplete' message. This is the failure-closed posture: medchat would rather say nothing than something it cannot back up.

If the gate is open, citecheck builds an EvidencePack from every tool result and walks the draft sentence by sentence. Any factual sentence that lacks a matching citation marker is stripped out. The remaining sentences form the cleaned output. A pack_hash is also computed, so the audit log can later prove which pieces of evidence were on hand for this turn.

Finally, citecheck observes the outcome. If a stub was used, the rolling 24-hour stub-rate ticks up. When that rate crosses 15%, auto-quiesce engages and every subsequent turn returns the stub until an operator manually calls POST /admin/quiesce/reopen.

flows.name: citecheck gate
flows.tagline: Every cloud answer passes through here. Strip uncited claims, count stubs, auto-quiesce if it gets bad.

flows.title: Local verify
flows.narration: MedGemma reads the cleaned draft and votes per sentence; the verifier never calls tools. The result is written to the audit row.

steps.narration: After citecheck has cleaned the draft, the response builder invokes /verify on the same draft and the same tool results. This is a second, independent opinion before any reply leaves the server.

medchat-mcp asks the local MedGemma model to read the draft alongside an evidence pack assembled from the turn's tool results. The system prompt tells MedGemma explicitly that it is a verifier — it must NOT rewrite anything, only score each sentence. The evidence pack is truncated to about 24,000 characters (roughly 6,000 tokens) so the prompt stays bounded.
steps.payload: model='medgemma-4b', system=VERIFIER_SYSTEM, draft + evidence pack (~24k char cap).

steps.narration: MedGemma returns a JSON list with one entry per sentence: {sentence_index, supported: true|false, reason: '...'}. medchat-mcp parses this into VerifierVerdict objects.

The verdicts are persisted on the audit row for this turn. The user-facing prose is never changed — verification is observation, not editing. This rule comes from ADR 0008: small models verifying is safe; small models rewriting is not.

flows.name: Local verify
flows.tagline: Per ADR 0008: MedGemma is a verifier, never a tool. It only reads the cleaned draft and votes per sentence.

flows.title: Admin reopen
flows.narration: After investigating, the operator POSTs to /admin/quiesce/reopen with the admin bearer token; the citecheck quiesce gate flips back to open.

steps.narration: When the operator has investigated an auto-quiesce and fixed the underlying problem, they reopen the gate by hand. The request is POST /admin/quiesce/reopen with header Authorization: Bearer ${MEDCHAT_ADMIN_TOKEN}. Without that token, the endpoint refuses.
medchat-mcp flips the in-process quiesce singleton from 'quiesced' back to 'open' and returns the new status along with the current stub-rate, so the operator can confirm the system is healthy again.

flows.name: Admin reopen
flows.tagline: After investigating why auto-quiesce engaged, the operator manually reopens the safety gate so normal answers can flow again.

flows.title: Audit turn
flows.narration: Every turn writes content_text and content_hash to medchat.turn in one statement; the nightly scrub will null content_text later.

steps.narration: After each turn, OpenWebUI is supposed to POST a complete audit record — conversation id, role (user or assistant), the raw content_text, the route used (local or cloud), token counts in and out, the tool calls made, and the evidence_pack_hash from citecheck. (Note: medchat-mcp implements the endpoint, but no in-repo OpenWebUI Function actually calls it yet — the glue is still TBD.)
steps.payload: {conversation_id, role, content_text, route, tokens, tool_calls, evidence_pack_hash}.

steps.narration: medchat-mcp inserts the row into medchat.turn. In the same INSERT statement, it also computes a SHA-256 hash of content_text and stores it in content_hash. This 'born together' rule is R4 in the TASKSPEC. Once the nightly scrub nulls content_text after 14 days, the hash still survives, so deduplication and integrity checks keep working.

flows.name: Audit turn
flows.tagline: Every turn writes content_text and content_hash atomically. The nightly scrub will null content_text later; the hash survives.

flows.title: Nightly ingest
flows.narration: Cron triggers the ingest container; it walks each corpus, skips unchanged chunks by content hash, embeds the new ones, and upserts rows in pgvector.

steps.narration: At 03:00 every night, the host's cron daemon fires the ingest job. The command is docker compose --profile ingest run --rm ingest python -m medchat_ingest delta-sync, with all output redirected to /var/log/medchat-ingest.log.
steps.payload: docker compose --profile ingest run --rm ingest python -m medchat_ingest delta-sync.

steps.narration: Docker spins up a fresh ingest container. The ingest compose profile keeps this container hidden from docker compose up — it only runs when cron asks for it. No restart, no healthcheck: it is single-shot by design.

Inside the container, six per-corpus chunkers (DailyMed, USPSTF, CDC, NIH/NHLBI, AAFP, WHO) fetch documents over HTTPS. Each chunker yields a SourceDoc plus its split-up chunks. A configurable maximum-items-per-corpus keeps a runaway scrape from filling the disk.

Before doing any expensive embedding work, ingest checks needs_reembed(corpus, external_id, content_hash) against PostgreSQL. If a document's content hash is unchanged from last run, the document is skipped entirely.

For chunks that actually need new embeddings, ingest calls Ollama at /api/embed using qwen3-embedding:8b. This is the same model used at query time, which is what makes query vectors and chunk vectors comparable.

The new chunks and their fresh embeddings are upserted into medchat_rag.source and medchat_rag.chunk. The query uses INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, so running ingest twice in a row produces the same end state — the operation is idempotent.

Before exiting, ingest prints a JSON summary of what it did (chunks added, embeddings created, items skipped, errors encountered). cron captures the line into /var/log/medchat-ingest.log, and the container shuts down.

flows.name: Nightly ingest
flows.tagline: While you sleep, the corpus refreshes. New chunks get embedded; unchanged ones are skipped by content hash.

flows.title: Audit scrub
flows.narration: Cron triggers the audit scrub task; rows older than MEDCHAT_AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS get content_text=NULL while their hashes survive.

steps.narration: At 04:00 every night, cron fires the audit scrub. The command is docker compose run --rm medchat-mcp python -m medchat_mcp.audit scrub, with output redirected to /var/log/medchat-scrub.log.
steps.payload: docker compose run --rm medchat-mcp python -m medchat_mcp.audit scrub.

steps.narration: Docker starts a throwaway medchat-mcp container. It uses the same image as the running sidecar, but instead of booting FastAPI it just runs the cli_scrub() function and exits.

The scrub runs a single SQL UPDATE: every row in medchat.turn older than MEDCHAT_AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS (default 14) has its content_text set to NULL. medchat.feedback.note gets the same treatment. The content_hash column is left untouched, so it survives as proof of what the row originally contained.
steps.payload: UPDATE medchat.turn SET content_text=NULL WHERE created_at < now() - interval '14 day'.

steps.narration: The CLI prints a JSON summary of how many rows were scrubbed. cron appends the line to /var/log/medchat-scrub.log, and the container shuts down.

flows.name: Audit scrub
flows.tagline: Privacy chore. After 14 days, content_text becomes NULL. The hash stays.

flows.title: VRAM watch
flows.narration: Every minute, verify-ceiling.sh asks ROCm for resident VRAM and appends a JSON line; crossing the threshold creates a sentinel file the monitor watches.

steps.narration: Every minute, cron runs the small shell script ops/verify-ceiling.sh. This is a plain script on the host — no Docker, no Python.
The script asks the AMD GPU directly: rocm-smi --showmeminfo vram. The number it returns is the resident VRAM in bytes, which in this setup is dominated by llama-server's model weights and KV cache.

The script appends one JSON line per minute to /var/log/medchat-vram.jsonl in the form {ts, used_gb, threshold_gb, alarm}. If used_gb exceeds MEDCHAT_VRAM_ALARM_GB (default 19), the script touches /tmp/medchat-alarm — a sentinel file that the homelab monitor watches. If usage falls back under the threshold, the script removes the sentinel.

flows.name: VRAM watch
flows.tagline: Every minute, a check. If VRAM crosses the threshold, the alarm sentinel appears.

flows.title: Deploy
flows.narration: docker compose up --build --force-recreate; medchat-mcp's healthcheck gates OpenWebUI, then alembic upgrade head runs the migrations.

steps.narration: The operator runs docker compose up --build --force-recreate. Compose builds the image medchat/medchat-mcp:0.5.0 from medchat-mcp/Dockerfile and starts medchat-mcp first. The container listens on port 8001 and exposes a /health healthcheck that runs every 30 seconds.

On container startup, the FastAPI lifespan handler opens the async SQLAlchemy engine pointed at MEDCHAT_DB_URL. The healthcheck endpoint then runs a trivial SELECT 1 against that engine, and only reports 'ok' once the database is reachable.

OpenWebUI is started only after medchat-mcp's healthcheck reports healthy — this is the depends_on: service_healthy contract in docker-compose.yml. The order matters: open-webui registers medchat-mcp as a tool server at startup, and a tool server that does not exist yet would cause a noisy failure on boot.

Finally, the operator optionally runs alembic upgrade head inside the medchat-mcp container. Every medchat migration uses IF NOT EXISTS guards, so running upgrade head against an already-up-to-date schema is a safe no-op.

flows.name: Deploy
flows.tagline: docker compose up --build --force-recreate. The healthcheck on medchat-mcp gates OpenWebUI.

flows.title: OWUI setup
flows.narration: ops/setup-openwebui.sh signs in, discovers the model list, and writes the medical system prompt plus the medchat-mcp tool server connection.

steps.narration: The setup script first authenticates against OpenWebUI. Either it POSTs the admin email and password to /api/v1/auths/signin, or it trusts a pre-issued WEBUI_TOKEN. Either way, it walks away with a bearer token that authorizes the rest of the calls.

Using that token, the script calls GET /api/models to discover which model aliases OpenWebUI currently knows about. The list comes from the two OpenAI base URLs configured on the container — one pointing at llama-server (the resident model) and one at nexus-router (cloud Claude).

Finally, the script POSTs configuration: the medical-disclaimer system prompt is pulled from ops/disclaimer-system-prompt.md (skipping the YAML front matter), and medchat-mcp is registered as an OpenAPI tool server pointing at http://medchat-mcp:8001. After this script finishes once, the workspace is ready.
steps.payload: Updates workspace; TOOL_SERVER_CONNECTIONS pointed at http://medchat-mcp:8001.

flows.name: OWUI setup
flows.tagline: ops/setup-openwebui.sh signs in, configures the medical system prompt, registers the tool server.

flows.title: Model download
flows.narration: ops/download-medgemma.sh pulls the Q4_K_M .gguf from HuggingFace into ./models, the directory shared with the sibling llama-server stack.

steps.narration: The operator runs ops/download-medgemma.sh, which downloads the MedGemma-4B-it weights from HuggingFace in the Q4_K_M quantization. Q4_K_M is a 4-bit k-quants build — small enough to fit comfortably in VRAM, accurate enough to be useful in medical context.

The downloaded .gguf file lands in ./models, which is bind-mounted into the sibling llama-server compose stack at ~/projects/llama-server. medchat keeps exactly one resident model at a time; swapping models is a manual scheduled-maintenance step, never something the runtime does on its own.

flows.name: Model download
flows.tagline: Download the resident model's weights once. The ./models directory is shared with the sibling llama-server stack, so both stacks see the same file.

flows.title: Bench gate
flows.narration: Every TASKSPEC bench gate runs in order; missing the VRAM ceiling, the latency target, or the harness rate halts the ship.

steps.narration: The day-one bench (ops/medchat-bench.sh) walks every TASKSPEC verification gate in order. It begins by asking llama-server to identify itself: GET /health to confirm it is alive, then GET /v1/models to confirm the expected model alias is being served.

Next, the script reads resident GPU memory via rocm-smi --showmeminfo vram. The bench fails the build if usage is above the 18 GB ceiling. A related limit (ADR 0008) applies inside the inference container at 14 GB.

Now the actual performance probe. ops/bench-tokps.py sends test prompts through /v1/chat/completions and records two numbers: the median tokens-per-second during generation, and the time-to-first-token. Acceptable values are tok/s ≥ 35 and TTFT ≤ 2.0 seconds.

On the medchat-mcp side, the script confirms the sidecar is healthy and that its database dependency reports 'ok'. Without a working database, audit writes would silently fail — that is a ship-blocker.

Finally, the cloud tool-call harness runs against nexus-router. It pushes 50 happy-path prompts plus at least 15 adversarial ones and grades whether the model chose the expected tool with the expected arguments. The bench fails if the pass-rate drops below 95%.

If every gate passes, the script appends a single row to BENCHMARKS.md recording the date and every measured metric. A missing row in BENCHMARKS.md is the audit trail's way of saying the bench refused to ship that build.

flows.name: Bench gate
flows.tagline: Every TASKSPEC gate, end to end. >15% regression fails the ship.

flows.title: Tool harness
flows.narration: tests.tool_harness.runner replays 50 happy-path and 15+ adversarial prompts; pass rate is graded on tool selection alone, not tool execution.

steps.narration: The harness lives in tests/tool_harness/runner.py. The operator runs it inside a throwaway medchat-mcp container: docker compose run --rm medchat-mcp python -m tests.tool_harness.runner --route cloud --prompts ops/tool-harness-prompts.json.
steps.payload: docker compose run --rm medchat-mcp python -m tests.tool_harness.runner --route cloud.

steps.narration: For each prompt, the harness sends a single /v1/chat/completions call to nexus-router, attaching the full TOOL_DEFS catalogue. It grades only the model's tool selection — did it pick the expected tool, and do its arguments match the expected regex? Whether the upstream API actually succeeded is out of scope; that is covered by per-tool integration tests.

When the harness finishes, it prints a JSON report with the total pass-rate, the per-tool pass-rate, and the per-prompt detail. The 95% ship gate is read straight from this number. The contract that at least three fresh adversarial prompts must rotate in each release is checked separately, by inspecting ops/harness-adversarial-prompts.json.

flows.name: Tool harness
flows.tagline: Grades tool selection, not execution. 50 happy-path + 15+ adversarial prompts.

glossary.OIDC: OpenID Connect. The auth protocol behind the medchat session cookie; the OIDC redirect URI is configured on OpenWebUI.
glossary.Cloudflare Tunnel: An outbound connection from the homelab to Cloudflare's edge. Exposes medchat.peyman.io without opening any inbound ports.
glossary.Traefik: The reverse proxy that routes Host=medchat.peyman.io to the open-webui container inside the platform-net Docker network.
glossary.platform-net: Shared external Docker network. medchat-mcp and open-webui both attach to it, plus Traefik.
glossary.OpenAI API: The OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions HTTP shape. llama-server and nexus-router both speak it; OpenWebUI calls them through the same shape.
glossary.SSE: Server-Sent Events. One-way streaming HTTP push used for both OpenAI streaming responses and the MCP /mcp endpoint.
glossary.strip_tool_chips: OpenWebUI outlet filter that removes <details type='tool_calls'> blocks from assistant messages before they're rendered.
glossary.citation_links: OpenWebUI outlet filter that rewrites markers like [PubMed:12345] into numbered hyperlinks and appends a Sources panel.
glossary.OpenAPI: The auto-generated JSON schema FastAPI exposes at /openapi.json. OpenWebUI reads it to discover medchat-mcp's tool endpoints.
glossary.tool server: OpenWebUI integration that reads a remote OpenAPI spec and offers its endpoints as model tools.
glossary.ToolResult: medchat-mcp's normalized response shape: { results: [...], note?: '...' }. Tools never 5xx — degraded calls return an empty results list with a note.
glossary.TOOL_SERVER_CONNECTIONS: Env on the open-webui container. Lists external OpenAPI tool servers to auto-register at startup.
glossary.PubMed: The NCBI literature database. medchat-mcp's pubmed_search calls the E-utilities API.
glossary.NCBI E-utilities: The HTTP search API for PubMed.
glossary.nexus-router: External OpenAI-compatible cloud router. medchat-mcp posts /v1/chat/completions to it with model='claude-sonnet-4-6'.
glossary.Claude Sonnet: claude-sonnet-4-6. The cloud LLM that runs the medchat-mcp tool-calling loop.
glossary.TOOL_DEFS: OpenAI-style function definitions medchat-mcp passes to the cloud model so it can choose which tool to call.
glossary.citecheck: The egress gate inside medchat-mcp. Resolves citation markers against the EvidencePack and strips uncited claims.
glossary.EvidencePack: A per-turn collection of tool results that citecheck inspects to validate every claim in the draft.
glossary.stub: The fallback 'evidence-incomplete' response served when citecheck cannot back up enough of the draft.
glossary.stub-rate: Rolling 24-hour fraction of turns served as stubs. Above 15% triggers auto-quiesce.
glossary.auto-quiesce: Failure-closed mode. While quiesced, citecheck always returns the stub until POST /admin/quiesce/reopen is called.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol. The standard for exposing tools to LLM clients. medchat-mcp serves /mcp via FastMCP SSE.
glossary.FastMCP: Python framework for MCP servers used by medchat-mcp; mounted under /mcp.
glossary.pgvector: PostgreSQL extension for vector similarity. medchat_rag.chunk.embedding is halfvec(4096).
glossary.halfvec: pgvector's half-precision (float16) vector type. Used by medchat_rag to cut storage in half.
glossary.cosine kNN: k-nearest-neighbor search by cosine similarity, expressed as ORDER BY embedding <=> halfvec(:qv).
glossary.qwen3-embedding: The 8B-param embedding model running on the Ollama daemon. Produces 4096-d vectors.
glossary.Ollama: Host-resident embedder daemon (port 11434). medchat-mcp and ingest both call its /api/embed endpoint.
glossary.files-service: Separate service that stores user uploads and serves /v1/files/{id}/retrieve with its own sqlite-vec retrieval.
glossary.sqlite-vec: Vector-search extension for SQLite; used inside files-service for per-file kNN.
glossary.MedGemma: The 4B medical specialist model running on llama-server. Per ADR 0008, used only as a post-draft verifier.
glossary.ADR 0008: Architecture decision: MedGemma is invisible to the cloud orchestrator. Triggered by the 2026-05-10 GPU fault.
glossary.verifier: A pass that reads the cleaned draft and the evidence, votes per sentence, and never rewrites the prose.
glossary.evidence pack: The truncated tool-results blob (~24k chars max, 6000 tokens) handed to the verifier.
glossary.MEDCHAT_ADMIN_TOKEN: Required Bearer token to call /admin/quiesce/reopen. No token, no reopen.
glossary.content_hash: SHA-256 over content_text. Survives the 14-day scrub so dedup and audits keep working.
glossary.content_text: Raw turn text. Nulled by the nightly scrub after MEDCHAT_AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS (default 14).
glossary.R4: TASKSPEC rule: content_hash MUST be computed in the same insert that writes content_text.
glossary.delta-sync: Ingest mode: re-fetch every corpus item but skip embedding when content_hash is unchanged.
glossary.profile: Docker Compose profile [ingest]. Keeps the ingest service out of `docker compose up` by default.
glossary.chunker: Per-corpus parser (dailymed.py, cdc.py, uspstf.py, ...) that yields SourceDoc + chunks.
glossary.idempotent upsert: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE. Running the same ingest twice produces the same row state.
glossary.retention: MEDCHAT_AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS, default 14. content_text older than this is nulled by the nightly scrub.
glossary.rocm-smi: Command-line tool that reads AMD GPU stats. medchat polls VRAM with --showmeminfo vram.
glossary.sentinel: /tmp/medchat-alarm. Touched when VRAM exceeds the ceiling; watched by homelab-monitor.
glossary.MEDCHAT_VRAM_ALARM_GB: Threshold for the alarm sentinel; default 19 GB.
glossary.depends_on: Docker Compose option. service_healthy form blocks startup until the upstream healthcheck reports healthy.
glossary.healthcheck: Compose healthcheck on medchat-mcp pings /health every 30s.
glossary.alembic: SQLAlchemy migration tool. All medchat migrations are idempotent (IF NOT EXISTS).
glossary.WEBUI_TOKEN: An OpenWebUI API key. Alternative to admin email+password sign-in for the setup script.
glossary.gguf: Quantized model file format used by llama.cpp. e.g. ./models/MedGemma-4B-it.Q4_K_M.gguf.
glossary.Q4_K_M: Mid-sized 4-bit quantization. The MedGemma file used by llama-server.
glossary.tok/s: Tokens per second produced by llama-server during generation.
glossary.TTFT: Time to first token. The bench gate requires TTFT <= 2.0 s.
glossary.VRAM ceiling: Resident VRAM limit checked by the bench gate. Above the threshold fails the ship.
glossary.tool selection: The cloud harness grades only which tool the model picks, not whether the upstream API actually succeeds.
